title: T2 · LEAP - jump to an address and run it
description: Wozmon's ADDR R form. Cast an address to a function pointer and call it. Combined with POKE this means you can type machine code in hex and execute it, which is the whole reason Wozmon mattered on the Apple I.
acceptance_criteria: POKE a few instructions that print a character and return, then LEAP to them.
close_reason: Tier 2 complete. All 10 acceptance criteria in WOZMON.md section 9 verified against a running kernel: examine one, ranges with left-padded short first row, .END continuation, store and store-continue, R runs typed-in machine code and returns, several commands per line, all five positioned errors with memory provably unchanged, backspace at an empty prompt, and the 129th character dropped without discarding the line.

title: T2 · SCAN - print a range of memory
description: Wozmon's ADDR.ADDR form. Print every byte between two addresses, in rows, with each row prefixed by its own address. Wrap sensibly and stop at the end address.
acceptance_criteria: A range spanning several rows prints with correct addresses and no missing bytes.
close_reason: Tier 2 complete. All 10 acceptance criteria in WOZMON.md section 9 verified against a running kernel: examine one, ranges with left-padded short first row, .END continuation, store and store-continue, R runs typed-in machine code and returns, several commands per line, all five positioned errors with memory provably unchanged, backspace at an empty prompt, and the 129th character dropped without discarding the line.

title: T2 · POKE - write bytes into memory
description: Wozmon's ADDR: XX XX XX form. Parse a list of hex byte values and store them, advancing the address. This is the point where the console can change the machine, not just observe it.
acceptance_criteria: Write a few bytes, then SCAN them back and see what you wrote.
close_reason: Tier 2 complete. All 10 acceptance criteria in WOZMON.md section 9 verified against a running kernel: examine one, ranges with left-padded short first row, .END continuation, store and store-continue, R runs typed-in machine code and returns, several commands per line, all five positioned errors with memory provably unchanged, backspace at an empty prompt, and the 129th character dropped without discarding the line.

description: Turn a string of hex digits into a u64. Accept upper and lower case, stop cleanly at the first non-digit, and reject input that is too long. This is half of Wozmon; the other half is printing hex, which core::fmt gives you free.
acceptance_criteria: Round trip: parse a typed address, print it back with {:#x}, and get the same text.
close_reason: Tier 2 complete. All 10 acceptance criteria in WOZMON.md section 9 verified against a running kernel: examine one, ranges with left-padded short first row, .END continuation, store and store-continue, R runs typed-in machine code and returns, several commands per line, all five positioned errors with memory provably unchanged, backspace at an empty prompt, and the 129th character dropped without discarding the line.

title: T2 · PEEK - print the byte at an address
description: Given a parsed address, read one byte and print it as two hex digits, in Wozmon's ADDR: XX format. The first command that makes the machine inspectable from its own console.
acceptance_criteria: Typing the address of a known byte in .rodata prints the right value.
close_reason: Tier 2 complete. All 10 acceptance criteria in WOZMON.md section 9 verified against a running kernel: examine one, ranges with left-padded short first row, .END continuation, store and store-continue, R runs typed-in machine code and returns, several commands per line, all five positioned errors with memory provably unchanged, backspace at an empty prompt, and the 129th character dropped without discarding the line.

title: T2 · LINE - read a line of input with echo and backspace
description: Read characters into a fixed-size buffer until Enter. Echo each one back so typing is visible, handle backspace by removing from the buffer and erasing on screen, and refuse to overflow the buffer. No allocation - a fixed array and a length.
acceptance_criteria: Typing a line with mistakes and corrections yields the corrected text.
close_reason: read_line in src/console.rs: fixed buffer, echo, backspace with BS SP BS, overflow reported as a flag. Verified by feeding 'hxe\x7f\x7fello' and getting 'hello'.

title: T1 · PANIC SPEAKS - make the panic handler print
description: The panic handler is currently 'loop {}', so every panic is a silent hang indistinguishable from a fault loop. Once fmt::Write exists, print the panic message and its file and line, then flush, then halt.
acceptance_criteria: A deliberate panic!("test") prints its message and location over serial.
close_reason: Panic handler builds its own UARTDriver, re-inits, prints a banner plus Display for PanicInfo (file:line:col + message), flushes, then parks on wfi. Reentrancy guarded by a static AtomicBool using load/store Relaxed - not swap, because load/store-exclusive on Device memory is CONSTRAINED UNPREDICTABLE with the MMU off. Verified with a deliberate panic in a scratch copy. .text 816 -> 6204 once a panic is reachable.

title: T1 · FLUSH - drain the transmit FIFO before stopping
description: Poll the BUSY flag in FR until the last character has physically left the wire. FIFO-empty and not-busy are different things: empty means you handed everything over, not-busy means the wire is quiet. Without this, the final message dies in the FIFO on halt or reset.
acceptance_criteria: A message printed immediately before SHUTDOWN still appears in full.
close_reason: flush() spins on FR BUSY, called in kmain after the last putc and before shutdown(). Verified inlined to a single tbnz loop immediately before hvc. QEMU never sets BUSY so it is unobservable there; it matters on hardware where 16 bytes is ~1.4ms of shifting.

title: T1 · SHUTDOWN - exit QEMU cleanly with PSCI SYSTEM_OFF
description: QEMU's virt machine implements PSCI, the ARM power interface. Calling SYSTEM_OFF with the HVC instruction makes QEMU exit instead of spinning forever. Turns every scripted test into something that terminates on its own.
acceptance_criteria: A kernel that calls it returns control to the shell with no kill needed.
close_reason: shutdown() calls PSCI SYSTEM_OFF (0x84000008) via HVC. Verified: QEMU exits on its own with stdin still open, no kill needed.

title: T1 · IDLE - wfi in the park loop
description: The kernel currently ends in 'b .', a busy spin. QEMU cannot tell that from real work, so every running instance pins a full host CPU core. The wfi instruction parks the core until an interrupt arrives, which costs nothing and is what a real idle loop does.
acceptance_criteria: Every path that parks the core uses wfi in a loop rather than a busy branch. Currently that is the panic handler in src/main.rs. Not observable as a host-CPU drop yet: kmain is divergent so the assembly park loop in kernel.s is unreachable, and nothing panics in the normal path. The idle-waiting-for-input path is a separate problem - getc busy-polls FR at ~99% host CPU and needs interrupts (Tier 2) to fix.
close_reason: wfi park loop implemented in the panic handler. Not yet observable - no panic in the normal path.

title: T1 · LANGUAGE - implement core::fmt::Write
description: One required method, write_str, built from putc in about three lines. In exchange you get write!/writeln! with hex, padding and alignment from core, with no allocation. Needed before Wozmon, which is entirely a hex parsing and printing program.
acceptance_criteria: write!(uart, "{:#010x}", value) prints correctly.
close_reason: impl core::fmt::Write for UARTDriver in src/uart.rs; write_str iterates as_bytes and emits \r before every \n. Verified: writeln!(uart, "Test: {:#010x}", 42u32) prints 0x0000002a. Costs 4172 bytes of .text; gated behind the debug-print Cargo feature so a --no-default-features build drops back to 240.

title: T1 · EARS - getc, the receive path
description: Poll FR for RXFE (bit 4) clear, then read DR and mask the low byte. Two functions: a non-blocking one returning Option<u8> and a blocking wrapper. Reading DR is destructive - the byte leaves the FIFO. Bits 8-11 of DR are per-byte framing/parity/break/overrun error flags.
acceptance_criteria: make feed INPUT='abc' echoes the characters back.
close_reason: getc + try_getc implemented, echo loop in kmain. 288 bytes fed in, 288 identical bytes back, zero drops.

title: T1 · CALIBRATE - UART init sequence
description: Disable the device, wait for BUSY to clear, flush the FIFOs by clearing FEN, write IBRD/FBRD, then write LCR_H (which is what latches the divisors), mask interrupts and clear pending, finally enable with UARTEN|TXE|RXE.
acceptance_criteria: make mem ADDR=0x09000024 N=4 FMT=xw reads back 0d 01 70 0301.
notes: Order is not negotiable: writing LCR_H latches IBRD/FBRD, so the divisors must be written first. Baud is computed at compile time with integer math: SCALED_DIVISOR = (4*UARTCLK + BAUD/2)/BAUD, then /64 and %64. No floats - f64::round does not exist in core and FP traps until CPACR_EL1 is configured.
close_reason: Closed

title: T1 · VOICE - putc with transmit flow control
description: Poll FR until TXFF (bit 5) is clear, then write the byte to DR. Wait for not-full, not for empty - waiting for empty throws away what the FIFO buys you.
acceptance_criteria: Hello prints over serial with the flow-control check in place.
notes: The read of FR must be INSIDE the loop. Hoisting it out gave the compiler a loop whose condition could never change, and it compiled the wait into 'b .' - a bare infinite loop. Confirmed in the disassembly: the tbnz target went from a dead spin to the ldrb itself once fixed.
close_reason: Closed

title: T2 · WORKBENCH - Wozmon
description: Port Steve Wozniak's 256-byte Apple I monitor, the one Ben Eater ports to his 6502. Read a hex address over serial and print the byte, print a range, write bytes into memory, jump to an address and run it. Needs nothing but the UART, and becomes the interactive debugging console for every later milestone.
acceptance_criteria: Can inspect memory, write memory, and jump to code from the serial console.
close_reason: Tier 2 complete. All 10 acceptance criteria in WOZMON.md section 9 verified against a running kernel: examine one, ranges with left-padded short first row, .END continuation, store and store-continue, R runs typed-in machine code and returns, several commands per line, all five positioned errors with memory provably unchanged, backspace at an empty prompt, and the 129th character dropped without discarding the line.

title: T1 · SIGNAL - a real PL011 UART driver
description: Replace the raw store with a driver in src/uart.rs: a struct holding the base address, private read_register/write_register wrapping volatile access, and named constants grouped in reg/fr/lcr_h/cr/icr modules. Covers init, transmit with flow control, and receive.
acceptance_criteria: init, putc and getc all work, verified by reading registers back with make mem rather than by looking at output.
close_reason: init, putc, getc, flush, core::fmt::Write and the RX error flags are all in src/uart.rs and were verified by reading registers back with make mem.

title: T0 · GROUND - linker script, where code, data and bss land
description: Write linker.ld: ENTRY(_start), place .text/.rodata/.data/.bss at RAM base 0x40000000, and plant __bss_start / __bss_end / __stack_top symbols that assembly can read. The script decides placement, not membership - source must use .section to put data somewhere.
acceptance_criteria: linker.ld drives layout; make sections/syms show the expected addresses.
close_reason: Closed

title: T0 · FOOTING - stack, .bss zeroing, jump into no_std Rust
description: src/kernel.s sets sp from __stack_top, zeroes .bss with a str xzr, [x0], #8 loop, then bl kmain. main.rs is #![no_std] with a #[panic_handler] and #[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern C kmain. MMIO writes must use core::ptr::write_volatile or the compiler deletes them.
acceptance_criteria: make test-bss passes: .bss poisoned with 0xAA before boot comes back zeroed, guard word past __bss_end untouched.
notes: Two real bugs found here: the zeroing loop was a do-while (store between test and branch), and then had an inverted condition (b.lo instead of b.hs). Both passed the naive check because QEMU hands you zeroed RAM - the poison-and-guard test is what caught them.
close_reason: Closed

title: T0 · SPARK - print a character by storing a byte to the UART
description: The hello world of bare metal. The PL011 UART sits at 0x0900_0000 on the virt machine; storing a byte to it emits a character on the serial line. Memory-mapped I/O, the software equivalent of wiring a chip to an address decoder.
acceptance_criteria: A character appears on the serial console from a raw store.
close_reason: Closed

title: T0 · FIRST BREATH - a few instructions in an ELF, under the debugger
description: Get a handful of aarch64 instructions into an ELF that QEMU will load with -kernel, and watch them execute under the debugger. Nothing printed yet. Established that lldb talks to QEMU's gdb stub via gdb-remote localhost:1234.
acceptance_criteria: Kernel loads, PC lands on _start, single-stepping works.
close_reason: Closed

title: T0 · OBSERVE - QEMU basics, machine models, the monitor
description: Understand what a QEMU machine model is, boot something, and learn to drive the monitor: info mtree -f, info registers, info qtree, xp, system_reset. Ctrl-A C toggles monitor, Ctrl-A X quits.
acceptance_criteria: Can explain what -M virt gives you and read the flat memory map from the monitor.
close_reason: Closed

title: SIDE · PLUMBING - one owner for the UART, one table for interrupts
description:
Two structural problems found right after the GIC came up, before any real device interrupt exists.

1. UARTDriver::new() is called at four sites (kmain, panic_handler, handle_interrupt, and via zhemon). Nothing guarantees init() ran, there is no place to hang a TX buffer for zheos-0hg, and once interrupts are live the IRQ handler prints on top of whatever zhemon is printing. Two writers, one device.

2. The interrupt path has no shape. gic::init() unmasks DAIF itself, so interrupts go live before any device is configured; it only works because nothing is wired up yet. handle_interrupt hardcodes what to do with an INTID. Adding a second interrupt source means editing the dispatcher.

Also fold in two latent bugs found during the GIC work:
  - vectors.s restore_all_registers uses 'ldp x30, x31' against a save side that used 'str x30'. Reads 8 bytes never written; xzr discards them, so harmless but asymmetric.
  - gic::acknowledge_interrupt masks the IAR value with 0x3FF before it reaches EOIR. Bits 12:10 carry the sending core for SGIs and EOIR wants them. Fine on one core.
design:
UART: one static owner, borrowed through a closure that masks IRQs for its duration (read DAIF, set I, run, restore). Single core means that is the whole critical section. The panic handler and the fault reporter must NOT take that lock - they need a raw path that talks to the hardware directly, or a panic while holding it deadlocks exactly when output matters most.

Interrupts: gic becomes a driver with no policy - enable, acknowledge, eoi, and no DAIF. A new irq module owns an array of handler slots indexed by INTID (64 slots covers SGI, PPI and the low SPIs) plus register(intid, handler) which fills a slot and enables it. handle_interrupt becomes ack, index, call, eoi, forever.

kmain reads as five phases, each needing the one above:
  1 uart init  2 install_vectors  3 gic::init  4 devices register handlers  5 irq::enable (the daifclr, last, on its own line)

Deliberately NOT doing: no irqchip trait or GICv3 abstraction (one implementation, extract it when v3 actually arrives); no device-tree discovery of base addresses; no priority levels or nesting.
acceptance_criteria: Manual SGI 0 still prints its line and the monitor still echoes afterwards. Nothing constructs a UART driver except the one owner. handle_interrupt contains no INTID-specific code. daifclr appears exactly once, in kmain's last phase.
notes:
DONE. Commits: 3872cdd print!/println! macros, 7da3886 UART singleton, d451718 putc_unsafe dropped.

The DESIGN section above is wrong about the lock and stayed wrong until the code was written. It called for borrowing the UART through a closure that masks IRQs. There is no lock and none was needed: UARTDriver holds only a base address, every method takes &self, and every write is a volatile store to a device register. Two writers cannot corrupt each other - the worst case is interleaved output. So the singleton is a plain 'static UART: UARTDriver' plus 'uart() -> &'static UARTDriver', with 'impl Write for &UARTDriver' so a shared reference can be formatted into. No unsafe, no UnsafeCell, no critical section.

That also killed the scary consequence recorded below. read_line spinning in getc() was only a problem because a lock held across it would mask interrupts until a human typed. No lock, no problem. The estimate of 'an afternoon' was wrong for the same reason.

putc_unsafe went with it - it existed so the fault path would not build and init a driver, and uart() needs neither.

Two real fixes fell out. handle_exception no longer calls uart.init(), which writes IMSC=0 and would have silently switched off UART interrupts the moment zheos-0hg turns them on. And write!(uart, "...\r\n") was being doubled to \r\r\n by write_str, which inserts \r before every \n; the println! conversion removed the explicit one. Verified by diffing full boot output against HEAD - byte-identical apart from that.

OUTSTANDING, carried to zheos-0hg or a follow-up: the macros in src/std.rs expand to bare 'uart()' and bare 'write!', not $crate-qualified paths. They compile today only because main.rs has a private 'use crate::uart::uart;' at the crate root, which child modules can see. Commenting out that one line breaks console.rs, exception.rs and zhemon.rs. Also println!() with no arguments does not compile, and the expansion is two loose statements rather than a block, so it cannot be used in expression position (a match arm).
close_reason: UART singleton landed; the lock the design called for turned out to be unnecessary

title: SIDE · Bare R runs the wrong address after an examine
description: WOZMON.md 4.1 says examining sets the current address to the address named, and 4.6 says a bare R runs the current address. handle_examine_one ends with current_address += 1, so after '\40020000' a bare R on the next line targets 40020001 and dies on the alignment guard. Typing '40020000 R' on one line works, because the parser emits SetAddress rather than ExamineOne and never increments.
design: current_address means 'where the next continuing operation starts'; the spec's current address means 'the last address named or touched', with the +1 applied at the point of use. Both models are self-consistent - the continuing commands are all correct, verified against 4.3 and 4.5. handle_run is the only place written against the spec's meaning while reading a field holding the other. Flipping the field wholesale does not work: SetAddress followed by a store must write the first byte AT the named address (4.4), so SetAddress would have to store address-1 and underflow at 0. Preferred fix: rename the field to next_address and add a second field for the last address named or touched, read only by handle_run. Alternative: drop bare R, which is a DECISION in the spec and not in the Apple I original.
acceptance_criteria: After '\40020000' on its own line, a bare R on the next line runs the code at 40020000. The one-line form still works, and the dot- and colon-continuing commands still match the 4.3 and 4.5 examples.
close_reason: Vector table installed and verified; bare R fixed with the two-field split and all five monitor cases re-tested.

title: SIDE · PROVING GROUND - a test harness for a no_std kernel
description:
Learn how to test bare-metal code, and what separates a good test from a test that merely exists. Right now every check in this project has been run by hand: boot QEMU, type things, read the screen. That does not scale and it does not catch regressions.

Two obstacles are already measured on stable 1.97.1:
  cargo test                               -> E0463: can't find crate for `test` (the built-in harness needs std)
  cargo test --target aarch64-apple-darwin -> E0152: duplicate lang item `panic_impl`

So the built-in harness cannot run on the bare-metal target at all, and running it on the host means cfg-gating the panic handler, no_main and the global_asm. custom_test_frameworks would solve it but is nightly-only.
design:
Three approaches, with what each can reach:

A. Host unit tests for the pure logic (parser, cursor, hex, InputChar). Gate the bare-metal items behind cfg(not(test)) and run with --target aarch64-apple-darwin. Unusually safe here because host and target are both little-endian 64-bit aarch64, so integer and pointer semantics are identical. Cannot reach the UART or mem::read_byte.

B. In-kernel self-test booted on the real machine, reporting over the UART and exiting QEMU with a status code via semihosting (SYS_EXIT 0x18 through hlt #0xf000, with -semihosting on the command line). PSCI SYSTEM_OFF carries no exit code, so it cannot fail a build. Reaches everything, but a test running inside the thing under test cannot detect a hang.

C. Golden transcript tests from outside: feed scripted keystrokes into QEMU, diff against a recorded expected output. Maps one-to-one onto WOZMON.md section 9, which is already a written test plan. Catches hangs if given a timeout. Brittle to cosmetic output changes and slow.

Recommendation: A plus C. Defer B until Tier 3, when exception handlers and interrupts exist that the host genuinely cannot run.
acceptance_criteria: make test runs without a human watching, exits nonzero when something is wrong, and each of the six known Tier 2 bugs is caught by at least one test that was seen to fail before it was seen to pass.
notes:
TRIGGER POINTS (decided after Tier 2, deliberately deferred):

1. Before starting zheos-0hg (UART IRQ), record a golden transcript of the current monitor. UART IRQ replaces the receive path underneath read_line, so a recorded transcript of the known-good Tier 2 monitor is a regression net aimed at exactly that change. Cheap: one shell script, one expected-output file.

2. Build the host unit-test harness (cfg-gating + cargo test --target aarch64-apple-darwin) when building the ring buffer in zheos-0hg. A concurrent producer/consumer buffer is the first pure logic in the project that hand-testing cannot cover: lost byte on wrap, full-vs-empty off-by-one, torn index.

3. Highest payoff is zheos-rel (TABLES). Turning the MMU on is the thing that breaks the ability to print, so a wrong page table entry makes the machine vanish with no output and no fault message. Building and checking tables on the host before loading TTBR0 is the difference between an afternoon and a week. zheos-gwp (DTB) is nearly as good a target because virt.dtb is already in the repo as real test input.

NOT BLOCKED BY ANYTHING. cargo test --target aarch64-apple-darwin works today once the panic_handler, no_main and global_asm are behind cfg(not(test)). Only #[test] on the bare-metal target is impossible on stable, and that needs nightly custom_test_frameworks, not a roadmap milestone.

Regression cases already known from real bugs found in Tier 2, each worth a test:
  - two bare addresses on one line printed only the last
  - . and R did not leave store mode, so '40010000: aa R 41' stored 41
  - parse_address returned Ok(0) on zero digits, silently examining address 0
  - a reverse range printed a stray blank line
  - an empty line infinite-looped in the validate pass
  - two caret off-by-ones on AddressTooLong and ByteTooLong

After writing any test, break the code on purpose and confirm the test goes red. A test that has never failed has never been tested.

title: T4 · BUMP - a bump allocator over free RAM
description: The simplest allocator that exists: a pointer to the next free byte, moved forward on each allocation, never freed. Enough to build page tables with, and enough to understand why real allocators are harder.
acceptance_criteria: Allocations return distinct, correctly aligned addresses inside the region DTB reported.

title: T4 · DTB - read the memory map from the device tree
description: QEMU leaves a pointer to the flattened device tree in x0 at entry, which kernel.s currently discards. Save it, parse the header, walk to the /memory node and read the real RAM base and size instead of hardcoding 0x40000000. The machine describing itself.
acceptance_criteria: Printed RAM base and size match what -m on the command line asked for.
notes: CORRECTION to the earlier premise note: there IS a live DTB at physical address 0x0 (the virt.flash0 pflash window) with plain -kernel kernel.elf, no -dtb and no generic loader. Verified magic 0xd00dfeed at 0x0, and the /memory size cell tracks -m: 0x08000000 at 128M, 0x10000000 at 256M, 0x20000000 at 512M. So the accurate claim is that QEMU gives an ELF kernel no way to FIND the device tree (x0=0), not that it provides none. My earlier search only covered RAM 0x40000000-0x48000000. 0x0 is not a promise - it is firmware's address whenever -bios/-pflash is used - so Path A/B still stand. Practical consequence: a parser that confuses blob offsets with absolute addresses reads valid tokens out of the copy at 0x0 and appears to half-work.

title: T3 · UART IRQ - interrupt-driven receive with a ring buffer
description: Stop polling for input. Unmask the receive and receive-timeout interrupts in IMSC, and have the handler drain the hardware FIFO into a software ring buffer. The timeout interrupt matters: without it, three characters sitting in a 16-deep FIFO never wake you and the terminal feels dead. Two buffers, deliberately: the 16-byte hardware FIFO you did not choose, and your ring buffer which can be any size. Handler does the minimum, main loop does the thinking.
acceptance_criteria: Typing while the main loop is busy loses nothing; getc reads from the ring buffer instead of polling FR.
close_reason: Interrupt-driven receive landed: e2ca35b, 6191217

title: T3 · TIMER - a periodic tick from the generic timer
description: The ARM generic timer is in the CPU, not on the bus. Read CNTFRQ_EL0 for its frequency, set CNTP_TVAL_EL0 for a countdown, enable it, and handle the interrupt by reloading it. The first thing that happens without the program asking, and the heartbeat everything above Tier 3 runs on.
acceptance_criteria: A counter incremented only by the timer handler visibly rises over time.
notes:
Guide written: TIMER.md at repo root. Verified on this machine: kernel runs at EL1h, CNTFRQ_EL0 = 0x3b9aca0 (62.5 MHz, NOT the UART's 24 MHz apb-pclk), CNTP_CTL_EL0/CNTP_CVAL_EL0/CNTFRQ_EL0 are readable over the gdb stub with lldb 'register read' (CNTPCT and TVAL are not).

Agreed interface, src/timer.rs:
  Stage 1 (the task): init(hz), ticks() -> u64, private handle_interrupt(u32). AtomicU64 + Relaxed for the counter, not UnsafeCell. hz = 100.
  Stage 2 (while the manual is open): now_us(), delay_us(), sleep_ms(). Counter half, no GIC involved; delay_us is the only timing primitive usable before IRQs are up.
  Stage 3 (not built): timer wheel, one-shot timers + callbacks, wall clock (that is PL031/zheos-kho), tickless, a Clock trait.

INTID 30 (PPI 14) goes in board.rs. gic.rs needs no change - gic::enable already skips ITARGETSR below 32.
Arm before enable (CVAL resets to 0 = deadline in the past). Re-arm before counting in the handler.
Start with TVAL, upgrade the reload to CVAL += interval once it ticks (drift, TIMER.md section 9).
close_reason: Periodic tick landed: CNTP_CVAL reload, Duration boundary, measured 99.997 Hz

title: T3 · VECTORS - install an exception vector table
description: VBAR_EL1 is 0 at reset, so any fault jumps to 0x200 in empty flash and the CPU fault-loops forever - the hang that looks like a hang. Build the 16-entry table with its required 128-byte spacing, point VBAR_EL1 at it, and make the synchronous handler print ESR_EL1 and FAR_EL1.
acceptance_criteria: A deliberate unaligned access or bad address prints its ESR and faulting address instead of hanging.
notes: Built as src/vectors.s (16-slot table, 2048-aligned, slots branch only) + src/exception.rs (install_vectors, ESRClass decode, ALREADY_FAULTED double-fault guard). Verified three ways: undefined instruction (EC 0x00, ELR at the run address), read of 0x1000000000000 (EC 0x25 data abort, FAR matches, DFSC 0 = address size fault), and a deliberate fault inside the handler (prints DOUBLE FAULT once, stops). Note: 0x20000000 does NOT fault on QEMU virt, it reads back 0xff - not a usable hole for testing. Deferred: separate handler stack via SPSel=0 + SP_EL1 (~6 lines) is pointless until the MMU can provide a guard page, so revisit at zheos-rel. Also deferred: DFSC/WnR decoding of the data-abort ISS, which is where decoding actually pays off from Tier 4 on.
close_reason: Vector table installed and verified; bare R fixed with the two-field split and all five monitor cases re-tested.

title: T3 · GIC - bring up the interrupt controller
description: GICv2: distributor at 0x08000000 decides which interrupts go where, CPU interface at 0x08010000 delivers them to this core. Enable both, set a priority mask that lets anything through, and unmask one interrupt ID. Until this is done, a device raising an interrupt changes nothing.
acceptance_criteria: An interrupt configured at the device actually reaches the handler installed by VECTORS.
close_reason: GIC up: distributor and CPU interface enabled, handler table dispatching, SGI reaches the handler and eret returns to a working monitor. Device-side enable (gate 1) belongs to zheos-0hg and zheos-ub4 by design.

title: T1 · RXERR - decode the receive error flags
description: Bits 8-11 of the data register are per-character error flags: framing, parity, break, overrun. Reading DR as a u8 throws them away. Overrun in particular means the FIFO filled and bytes were destroyed, which is the failure you most want to know about.
acceptance_criteria: getc can report which of the four errors, if any, arrived with a byte.
close_reason: Per-character DR error flags decoded into RxFlags, Display prints only the set flags. Break verified end-to-end with Ctrl-A b.

title: Chore: move the build to cargo and split out src/uart.rs
description: Was rustc --emit=obj plus a separate clang assembler step, linked by hand with rust-lld. Now cargo edition 2024: .cargo/config.toml pins the target, build.rs passes -Tlinker.ld with rerun-if-changed, kernel.s comes in via global_asm!(include_str!). The Makefile stays as the front end and copies the output to kernel.elf.
notes: Nested register modules referenced super::super::bit_mask, which breaks the moment module depth changes. crate::bit_mask is absolute from the crate root and survives moves.
close_reason: Closed

title: T4 · TERRITORY - device tree, bump allocator, the MMU
description: Read the physical memory map out of the device tree the bootloader hands over rather than hardcoding 0x40000000. Then a bump allocator, then the MMU and page tables. Turning the MMU on also removes the Device-memory alignment restriction that bites while it is off.
acceptance_criteria: Memory map discovered at runtime, allocation works, MMU enabled with translation tables.

title: T3 · REFLEX - exceptions, the vector table, the GIC
description: Install a vector table in VBAR_EL1, handle a synchronous exception properly instead of fault-looping, then bring up the GIC (distributor at 0x08000000, CPU interface at 0x08010000) and take a timer interrupt. Then convert the UART receive path from polling to interrupt driven.
acceptance_criteria: A deliberate fault reports its ESR instead of hanging, and a timer interrupt fires.
close_reason: Umbrella satisfied from below: vectors + ESR reporting (exception.rs), GIC bring-up (gic.rs), timer interrupt (zheos-ub4), UART IRQ receive (zheos-0hg) all landed

title: T5 · SCHED - round-robin on the timer tick
description: A task table, a current index, and a timer handler that picks the next runnable task and switches to it. Preemptive, because the tasks never agreed to yield. This is the line where it becomes a kernel.
acceptance_criteria: Two tasks printing different characters interleave without either calling into the scheduler.

title: T5 · SWITCH - save and restore a context
description: Save the callee-saved registers and the stack pointer of one task, load another's, and return into different code than you were called from. Assembly, unavoidably - this is the one place Rust cannot express what needs to happen.
acceptance_criteria: Two functions hand control back and forth by hand, each keeping its own locals.

title: T4 · HEAP - a GlobalAlloc so the alloc crate works
description: Implement core::alloc::GlobalAlloc over the allocator and declare it with #[global_allocator]. In exchange, extern crate alloc gives Box, Vec and String with no std. The first time this stops feeling like assembly with extra steps.
acceptance_criteria: A Vec grows and its contents survive.

title: T4 · MMU ON - enable the MMU and caches
description: Point TTBR0_EL1 at the tables, configure TCR_EL1 and MAIR_EL1, then set the M bit in SCTLR_EL1. The dangerous moment: the instruction after the enable is fetched through translation. Side effect worth watching for - the unaligned-access restriction disappears, because memory stops being Device memory.
acceptance_criteria: Kernel survives the enable and keeps printing; an unaligned load that previously faulted now works.

title: T4 · TABLES - build translation tables
description: Page tables for aarch64: a multi-level tree turning virtual addresses into physical ones. Map RAM as normal cacheable memory and the device region as device memory, identity mapped to start with so nothing moves the moment it turns on.
acceptance_criteria: Tables built and inspectable, MMU still off.
notes: From zheos-dmu (VECTORS): give the exception handler its own stack here. Mechanism is small - msr spsel, xzr so the kernel runs on SP_EL0, point SP_EL1 at a second stack, and move the real handler from vector slot 0x200 to 0x000 (the group is chosen by which SP was in use). Taking an exception forces SPSel=1, so the switch is free. Deliberately NOT done at zheos-dmu: without an MMU there is no guard page, so a stack overflow silently scribbles on .bss instead of faulting, and the separate stack protects against an exception that never gets raised. It starts paying once page tables can leave an unmapped guard page below the stack. Also worth adding here: decode the data-abort ISS - bit 6 WnR (read vs write) and bits 5:0 DFSC (0b0000LL address size, 0b0001LL translation, 0b0011LL permission, 0x21 alignment). Every MMU mistake arrives as a data abort and DFSC is the whole answer.

title: T5 · MANY HANDS - tasks and scheduling
description: The first thing that actually resembles a kernel: more than one thing running, context switching on the timer interrupt. Deliberately last - everything before it is prerequisites.
acceptance_criteria: Two tasks run concurrently, switched by the timer.

title: SIDE · TWO WORLDS - drop to EL0 and add syscalls
description: Run code at exception level 0 with no access to the hardware, and let it ask the kernel for things with the SVC instruction. The moment there is a privilege boundary, this stops being a program and starts being an operating system.

title: SIDE · MANY CORES - wake the secondary CPUs with PSCI
description: Boot with -smp 4 and use PSCI CPU_ON, via the SMC or HVC instruction, to start the other cores. Suddenly a single shared UART needs a lock, and every assumption about there being one thread of execution has to be revisited.

title: SIDE · HANDS - drive the PL061 GPIO controller
description: The pl061 GPIO controller at 0x09030000 is the closest thing on this machine to Ben Eater's 6522 parallel port: set pin directions, write pin values, read them back. Nothing physical is attached in QEMU, but the register discipline is identical.

title: SIDE · STORAGE - talk to a virtio-mmio block device
description: 32 virtio-mmio slots start at 0x0A000000, 0x200 apart. Negotiate features, set up a virtqueue, read one sector off a disk image. The first device that is not just registers: it needs shared memory rings, which is a genuinely new idea and needs an allocator first.

title: SIDE · TIMEKEEPER - read the PL031 real time clock
description: The pl031 RTC sits at 0x09010000. A second device with a register map, deliberately chosen because it is simple: read a counter, get wall-clock seconds. Practice at applying the driver pattern to a chip you have never seen, using only its TRM.

value: QEMU -kernel with an ELF gives no DTB *pointer*: x0=0, because the bootloader stub that would set it is only built on the is_linux path (raw images are assumed to be Linux kernels, ELFs are not). The blob itself IS generated and loaded. hw/arm/boot.c only sets info->dtb_start = loader_start when 'image_low_addr > loader_start || image_high_addr < loader_start'; linker.ld starts us at 0x40000000 == loader_start, so neither holds, dtb_start keeps its zero, and arm_load_dtb drops the tree at physical 0x0 (the virt.flash0 window). Verified: with -kernel, 0x0 = edfe0dd0 and 0x40000000 = our code; with no -kernel, 0x0 = zeroes and 0x40000000 = edfe0dd0. 0x0 is not a promise - it is firmware under -bios/-pflash. Use -device loader,file=virt.dtb,addr=...,force-raw=on instead.
Roadmap granularity: do not file beads issues for one-line changes. Fold them into the skill they belong to, or just do them. User asked for this after IDLE (a single wfi) got its own issue.
